In the 1680s he was arrested in the Marava country with his catechists, chained, tortured and finally expelled. Called back to Europe on the business of his province, he reached Lisbon about 1687. The king and the court wanted him to stay, and he is reported to have declined even an appointment as archbishop of Cranganore. He chose to return to India instead, and came back to the Tamil country around 1690 or 1691.

He went back to the Marava country, where a local prince, known in the accounts as Tadiya Thevan, sought baptism after an illness. John told him that a Christian may have only one wife, and the prince sent away his other wives. One of them, a niece of the ruler of Marava, complained to her uncle, and the missionary was arrested early in 1693. He was taken to Ramanathapuram and then to Oriyur, and there he was beheaded, on the date generally kept as 4 February 1693. His body was mutilated and left on a stake. He was beatified by Pope Pius IX and canonised by Pope Pius XII on 22 June 1947. A great shrine stands at Oriyur, where Christians and people of other faiths come to pray.
lessons: Becoming one with the people
He took on the language and the simple life of those he served, without changing the faith.
He chose to return
Court and honour were offered to him, and he went back to the poor and to danger.
Marriage is sacred
He died because he taught the truth of Christian marriage.
Catechists as partners
Lay people suffered and worked with him and carried the Gospel with him.
stories: Back in Portugal, John was urged by the court to remain, and he is said to have refused both comfort and high office. He returned to the land from which he had been expelled, knowing what he would probably face there.

When the prince asked for baptism, John could have looked the other way for the sake of a powerful convert. He did not. The dismissal of the prince's other wives brought about the complaint that led to John's death.
People at Oriyur say that the sand on the mound where he died turned red from his blood and has stayed red. Pilgrims still carry some of it home.
quotes: I await death, and I await it with impatience. It has always been the object of my prayers.
St John de Britto, letter to his superior before his death, 1693, in substance
p
johnbritto.prayer: Lord God, you gave St John de Britto courage to leave all things and to shed his blood for you in our land. Through his prayers, make us faithful to the truth of the Gospel and generous in bringing it to all people, with humility and love. Amen.

points: He gave up home and rank for Christ (Matthew 16:25).
He walked and lived as the people he served.
He would not compromise the teaching on marriage.
homily: Dear friends, St John de Britto could have lived comfortably at a royal court in Portugal. Instead he walked barefoot through the villages of the Tamil country, wore the simple robe of an Indian holy man, and spoke Tamil so well that people called him Arul Anandar. He belongs to the story of the faith in our land. His blood was shed on Indian soil, at Oriyur.

Jesus says: those who lose their life for my sake will find it (Matthew 16:25). John lived these words twice. He was expelled from the Marava country after chains and torture, and when he reached Lisbon, honours awaited him there. He could have stayed with an easy conscience, having suffered much already. He chose to go back, for he loved those people more than his own safety.

He was finally killed because of the truth about marriage. A prince wished to be a Christian, and John told him that a Christian husband has one wife. This cost him his life. In our time too, faithfulness in marriage may cost something. Let us thank God for husbands and wives who remain faithful, and for pastors who teach this truth with courage and with mercy.

When we come to the {Q} today, let us remember that this faith was handed on to us at great cost, by missionaries and by catechists whose names we do not know. Let us ask St John de Britto to give us his love for the poor, his respect for every people and culture, and his readiness to pay the price of the truth. Amen.

word: My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness.
2 Corinthians 12:9
life: Agatha was a young Christian woman of Sicily who died for her faith, probably in the middle of the third century, during the persecution of the emperor Decius, around 251. Catania and Palermo have both claimed her as a daughter of their city, and Catania, where she died, honours her as its patroness. Almost nothing else can be stated with certainty about her life. Her fame, however, is very old and well attested.

The Acts of her martyrdom were written later and cannot be taken as an exact record. They describe a young woman of good family who had consecrated her virginity to Christ. The Roman official Quintianus desired her, and when she refused him he had her accused as a Christian. He placed her in a house of ill repute to break her will, then had her tortured, and in the cruellest part of the torment had her breasts cut off. She died in prison.

Whatever may be uncertain in these details, the Church's memory of her is ancient. Her name appears in the early martyrologies, and it is still spoken in the Roman Canon, the First Eucharistic Prayer, alongside Felicity, Perpetua, Lucy, Agnes, Cecilia and Anastasia. In Rome, St Gregory the Great dedicated to her the church now known as Sant'Agata dei Goti. A sermon of St Methodius of Sicily, read in the Roman Office on her feast, plays on her name, which means good in Greek.

Catania celebrates her every February with one of the great processions of Italy. She is invoked against fire and against the eruptions of Mount Etna, and women suffering from diseases of the breast ask her prayers, as do nurses. Her story reminds us that the bodies of women are holy and that no violence can take from a person the dignity she has before God.
lessons: Dignity no one can take
Violence could wound Agatha's body, but it could not touch her dignity.
Belonging to Christ
Her promise to Christ, as the Acts present it, was stronger than power and fear.
Strength in weakness
A young woman stood firm before an official of the empire.
Compassion for those who suffer
She is a companion for women who are sick or who have suffered abuse.
stories: The Acts tell that on the night after her torture an old man came to Agatha in prison with medicine, revealed himself as the apostle Peter, and healed her wounds in the name of Christ.
People of Catania say that when Etna erupted about a year after her death, they carried her veil out against the lava and the flow stopped. Her veil is still carried in the city's procession.
From early times her name was included among the holy women named in the Roman Canon. Every priest who prays this Eucharistic Prayer still names this Sicilian girl.
quotes: Jesus Christ, Lord of all, you see my heart, you know my desires. Possess all that I am. I am your sheep: make me worthy to overcome the devil.
Prayer of St Agatha in the Acts of her martyrdom, in substance
p
agatha.prayer: Lord God, you gave St Agatha strength to stay faithful to you through cruel suffering. Through her prayers, protect all who are sick or wounded, comfort those who have suffered violence, and make us reverent toward the dignity of every person. Amen.

points: God's strength shone in her suffering (2 Corinthians 12:9).
Our bodies are holy; no one may treat a person as an object.
Her prayers for the sick and the wounded.
homily: Dear friends, we do not know many exact details about St Agatha, but we know that the Church has never forgotten her. For well over a thousand years, her name has been spoken in the Eucharistic Prayer at the {Q}. She was a young woman in Sicily who would not surrender herself to a powerful man and would not deny Christ.

The Lord says to St Paul: My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9). An official of the empire had every kind of power over Agatha, or so it seemed. He could imprison her and torture her. But he could not make her deny the Lord to whom she had given her life. Her story has outlived his.

Her story touches a painful subject. Women and girls still suffer harassment, abuse and violence. The Church must be a place where they are believed, protected and cared for, and our homes and parishes must be places where each person's dignity is respected. Let us say clearly today that no one who has suffered such things has lost her worth before God.

Let us also remember women with breast cancer and all who are ill, their families and those who nurse them. Many of them feel weak and afraid. May St Agatha pray for them, and may we stand beside them with our prayer and our practical help, so that they too may find that grace is sufficient. Amen.

word: May I never boast of anything except the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.
Galatians 6:14
life: The Gospel came to Japan with St Francis Xavier in 1549, and within a few decades there were many thousands of Japanese Catholics. Paul Miki was born in the 1560s into a well-to-do Japanese family and was baptised as a child. He was educated by the Jesuits, entered the Society of Jesus in the 1580s, and became known as a gifted preacher who could speak to Buddhists about Christ. He was close to ordination as a priest when he was arrested.

The ruler Toyotomi Hideyoshi had issued a decree against the missionaries in 1587, though at first it was not strictly enforced. In 1596 a Spanish ship, the San Felipe, was wrecked on the coast of Japan, and suspicion grew that missionaries were preparing the way for foreign conquest. In December of that year arrests began at Kyoto and Osaka.

Twenty-six were condemned: six Franciscan missionaries led by St Peter Baptist, three Japanese Jesuits including Paul Miki, and seventeen Japanese lay people, among them catechists, a doctor, craftsmen and boys as young as twelve or thirteen. Part of each one's left ear was cut off, and they were led through the towns on a journey of about a month to Nagasaki in the depth of winter, as a warning to Christians. They encouraged one another and those who came to see them, and they prayed along the way.

On 5 February 1597, on a hill overlooking Nagasaki, they were tied to crosses and pierced with lances. Paul Miki preached from his cross and forgave those who killed him. They were beatified in 1627 and canonised by Pope Pius IX on 8 June 1862. Fierce persecution followed for over two centuries, and priests could not stay in the country. The site of their death, Nishizaka, is now a place of pilgrimage. Because 5 February is the feast of St Agatha, the Roman calendar keeps their memory on 6 February.
lessons: The cross as a pulpit
Paul Miki went on preaching Christ while he was dying.
Forgiveness at the end
Like Jesus, he forgave his killers.
The whole Church bears witness
Priests and lay people, foreigners and Japanese, adults and children died together.
Faith handed down in the home
Parents and catechists kept the faith alive without priests for generations.
stories: An eyewitness account, read in the Roman Office on this day, says that Paul Miki told the crowd he was dying because he had preached Christ, that he forgave those who put him to death, and that he hoped his blood would fall on his people as fruitful rain.
The boy who ran to his cross

Accounts of the martyrdom tell of the youngest of them, Louis Ibaraki, a boy of about twelve. Offered his life if he would give up his faith, he refused. He is said to have run to his cross and asked which one was his.

In March 1865, soon after a Catholic church was opened in Nagasaki, a group of Japanese people came quietly to the French priest Bernard Petitjean and told him that they shared his faith. They asked him where the image of Holy Mary was. Their families had kept the faith in secret for over two hundred years without priests, by baptising and praying at home.
quotes: The only reason for my being killed is that I have taught the doctrine of Christ. After Christ's example I forgive my persecutors. I do not hate them. I ask God to have pity on all, and I hope my blood will fall on my fellow men as a fruitful rain.
St Paul Miki, from a contemporary account of the martyrdom, in substance
p
paulmiki.prayer: O God, strength of all your saints, you called St Paul Miki and his companions through the cross to eternal life. Through their prayers, grant that we may hold firmly to our faith until death and forgive those who hurt us. Amen.

points: They walked to Nagasaki unashamed of Christ (Galatians 6:14).
The hidden Christians kept the faith for two centuries.
homily: Dear friends, imagine the road to Nagasaki in the winter of 1597. Twenty-six Christians walk for about a month, wounded and watched by crowds, with boys among them. Those who sentenced them wanted to frighten the Christians of Japan. Instead the martyrs sang and preached along the way, and their road became a witness to Christ.

St Paul writes: May I never boast of anything except the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ (Galatians 6:14). Paul Miki made this his own. Tied to his cross, he told the people that he was dying because he had taught the doctrine of Christ. Then he said what is hardest of all: he forgave those who were killing him, and he hoped that his blood would fall on his people as fruitful rain.

That rain did fall. For over two centuries there were no priests in Japan. Yet when a French priest opened a church at Nagasaki in 1865, people came to him who had kept the faith in secret. Parents had baptised their children, taught them the prayers, and told them that one day priests would return. Mothers and fathers kept the Church alive.

We can come to the {Q} without fear. Let us not take that for granted. Let us pray for Christians who suffer for their faith today. Let us teach our children to pray at home, so that faith does not depend only on what happens in church. And when someone wounds us, let us remember Paul Miki on his cross and ask for the grace to forgive. Amen.

bakhita.t: Virgin, Canossian sister, once a slave
word: For freedom Christ has set us free. Stand firm, therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery.
Galatians 5:1
life: Bakhita was born around 1869 at Olgossa in Darfur, in present-day Sudan. When she was still a child, perhaps seven to nine years old, she was kidnapped by slave traders. The shock made her forget the name her parents had given her. Her captors called her Bakhita, an Arabic word meaning fortunate. She was sold and resold at the markets of El Obeid and Khartoum, and some of her owners treated her with great cruelty. One had her body cut with a razor and salt rubbed into the wounds, which left more than a hundred scars.

In 1883 the Italian consul at Khartoum, Callisto Legnani, bought her and treated her kindly. When he returned to Italy in 1885 she begged to go with him. In Italy she was given to the family of Augusto Michieli and became nursemaid to their small daughter, Mimmina. When Signora Michieli went to Sudan to join her husband in his business there, Bakhita and the child were entrusted to the Canossian Sisters in Venice, where she began to learn about the God she had sensed from her childhood.

When Signora Michieli came back to take her away, Bakhita, with great courage, refused to go. The case went to a court in Venice, and on 29 November 1889 it ruled that since slavery was not recognised in Italy, she had the right to decide for herself. She stayed with the Sisters, and on 9 January 1890 she received Baptism, Confirmation and First Communion from the Cardinal Patriarch of Venice, Domenico Agostini, taking the names Josephine Margaret Fortunata. In 1893 she entered the Canossian novitiate, and she made her vows on 8 December 1896.

From 1902 she lived in the convent at Schio, near Vicenza, where for over forty years she served as cook, sacristan, seamstress and doorkeeper. The townspeople loved her gentleness and called her their Moretta, the little brown sister. She told her story for the mission work of her congregation, and she died at Schio on 8 February 1947. Pope John Paul II beatified her in 1992 and canonised her on 1 October 2000. Pope Benedict XVI presented her as a witness of hope in his encyclical Spe Salvi, and since 2015 her feast has been a day of prayer and reflection against human trafficking.
lessons: Known and loved by God
She found out that she had a Master who loved her, not one who owned her.
Courage to say no
Before the court she stood up for her right to stay with God.
The dignity of humble work
A former slave served for decades as cook and doorkeeper and was at peace.
Mercy for the worst
She came to pray for those who had hurt her.
stories: Who is the master of the stars?

Bakhita later said that as a child she looked at the sun, moon and stars and wondered who their Master was. She felt a great desire to see him and to honour him, long before anyone told her about God.

In Benedict XVI's account in Spe Salvi, Bakhita had known many masters, cruel ones and kind ones. Then in Venice she heard of a master above all masters, the Lord who loved her and had suffered too. In the Venetian dialect she called him her Paron, her Master.

Sisters who nursed her at the end said that in her last illness, her mind going back to the slave days, she asked them to loosen the chains, because they were heavy. Then, it is reported, she said that she was very happy and that Our Lady had come.
quotes: If I were to meet those slave traders who kidnapped me, and even those who tortured me, I would kneel and kiss their hands; for if those things had not happened, I would not be a Christian and a religious today.
St Josephine Bakhita, reported words, in substance
p
I am definitively loved and whatever happens to me, I am awaited by this Love. And so my life is good.
Pope Benedict XVI, Spe Salvi 3, describing her faith, in substance
p
bakhita.prayer: God of mercy, you led St Josephine Bakhita from slavery to the dignity of a daughter of God. Through her prayers, break the chains of all who are trafficked and abused, give us courage to defend them, and teach us to trust in your love. Amen.

points: For freedom Christ has set us free
A slave who found the true Master (Galatians 5:1).
Whatever happens to me, this Love awaits me.
Her feast is a day of prayer against human trafficking.
homily: Dear friends, St Josephine Bakhita did not even remember the name her parents gave her. The name she carried was given by men who stole her as a child, and it meant fortunate. For years she was bought and sold, beaten and cut. If anyone had the right to believe that life had no meaning and that no one cared, it was she.

Yet in Venice she heard of a Master unlike all others: God, who knew her and loved her, and whose Son had also been beaten. Pope Benedict XVI writes that this changed her life. She knew she was definitively loved, and that whatever happened, this Love was waiting for her. St Paul says: For freedom Christ has set us free (Galatians 5:1). Long before the court in Venice ruled on her case, she was learning who truly owned her heart.

Bakhita asks us two questions. The first is about hope: do we live as people who know that they are loved? Many of us have everything and yet feel lost. The second is about our neighbour. Millions of people today are trafficked, forced into labour or the sex trade, or held as domestic workers with no rights. Some are close to us, in our cities and even in our homes. Let us see them. Let us pay fair wages and treat with respect those who work for us.

For more than forty years she cooked, sewed, and opened the convent door with a smile, and she was content. She even came to pray for those who had enslaved her. At this {Q}, let us thank God for her, and pray for all who are enslaved today, that they may find rescue, and that we may become their defenders. Amen.

lourdes.t: The apparitions to St Bernadette at Lourdes, World Day of the Sick
word: His mother said to the servants, “Do whatever he tells you.”
John 2:5
life: Bernadette Soubirous was born on 7 January 1844 at Lourdes, a small town in the Pyrenees in southern France. Her family had fallen into deep poverty and in 1857 were living in a single damp room in a former jail, known as the cachot. She was fourteen, often sick with asthma, and had not yet been able to make her First Communion, because she had had so little schooling.

On 11 February 1858, while gathering wood with her sister and a friend near the rock of Massabielle beside the river Gave, she saw in a hollow of the rock a young lady dressed in white, with a blue sash, a yellow rose on each foot and a rosary on her arm. Bernadette prayed the rosary, and the lady passed the beads through her fingers with her. Over the following months the lady appeared eighteen times, the last on 16 July 1858. Bernadette reported that she called for prayer and penance for sinners, that she had her scratch the ground and drink at a spring which then began to flow, and that she asked for a chapel to be built and for people to come in procession. On 25 March, the feast of the Annunciation, when asked her name, the lady answered in the local dialect: I am the Immaculate Conception. Bernadette did not understand the words. Pope Pius IX had defined that dogma in 1854.

Bernadette was questioned harshly by the police and by the local authorities, and at first with great suspicion by her parish priest, Abbé Peyramale. She never changed her account and never sought to gain from it. After a careful commission of inquiry, Bishop Bertrand-Sévère Laurence of Tarbes declared on 18 January 1862 that the faithful were justified in believing that Mary had appeared to her. Bernadette left Lourdes in 1866 to join the Sisters of Charity at Nevers, where she worked in the infirmary and sacristy, suffered much illness, and died on 16 April 1879, aged thirty-five. Pope Pius XI canonised her on 8 December 1933.

It is important to be clear about what this means. Apparitions are private revelation. As the Catechism teaches (CCC 67), they do not belong to the deposit of faith and do not add to Christ's definitive Revelation; they may help us to live by it more fully in a certain period of history. Catholics are not obliged to believe in Lourdes as they are obliged to believe the Creed. The doctrine of the Immaculate Conception does not depend on Lourdes. Lourdes is a place of Eucharistic adoration, confession, prayer and care for the sick. More than seventy cures have been recognised as miracles by the Church after strict medical and theological examination. In 1992 Pope John Paul II instituted the World Day of the Sick, to be kept each year on this date.
lessons: God chooses the little ones
A poor, sick girl who could barely read became the messenger.
Prayer and penance
What Bernadette heard is at the heart of the Gospel: conversion.
The sick come first
At Lourdes the sick go to the front and are served by others.
Rightly placed devotion
Private revelation never replaces the Gospel; Mary always points to her Son.
stories: The name she repeated all the way

When the lady gave her name on 25 March 1858, Bernadette did not know what it meant. She is said to have repeated the words again and again as she walked to the priest's house so as not to forget them. Abbé Peyramale was deeply shaken, for a girl like her could not have understood the expression.

On 25 February 1858, in front of the crowd, Bernadette scratched at the muddy ground as she said the lady had told her, and she tried to drink. People thought she had lost her mind. Over the next days, the trickle became the spring that still flows at Lourdes.
In later life Bernadette said that Our Lady had used her as one uses a broom, and that when the work is done the broom goes back behind the door. She was glad to be there.
quotes: We, therefore, judge that the Immaculate Mary, Mother of God, really appeared to Bernadette Soubirous, on 11 February 1858 and on the following days, and that the faithful are justified in believing this as certain.
Bishop Laurence of Tarbes, decree of 18 January 1862, in substance
p
I am not charged with making you believe it. I am charged with telling you.
St Bernadette, in substance
p

Private revelations do not belong to the deposit of faith. It is not their role to improve or complete Christ's definitive Revelation, but to help live more fully by it in a certain period of history.
Catechism of the Catholic Church 67, in substance
p
lourdes.prayer: Merciful God, grant us strength in our weakness. Through the prayers of the Immaculate Virgin Mary, Mother of God, and of St Bernadette, comfort the sick and those who care for them, and lead us to turn back to you in prayer and penance. Amen.

points: Mary's whole message points to Jesus (John 2:5).
CCC 67: a help for living the Gospel, not an addition to it.
The sick in the front row
Today is the World Day of the Sick.
homily: Dear friends, in 1858 God did not choose a learned person or a powerful family at Lourdes. He chose Bernadette, a poor and sickly girl of fourteen who lived with her family in a former jail. She said herself that if there had been anyone poorer or more ignorant, Our Lady would have chosen that person. This is how God works, as Mary herself sings in the Magnificat.

Let us be clear about what we celebrate. The apparitions of Lourdes are private revelation. The Church has examined them and permits us to trust them, as Bishop Laurence did in 1862, but they do not add anything to the faith. As the Catechism says, they help us to live more fully by Christ's Revelation (CCC 67). The Immaculate Conception is a dogma of the Church, defined in 1854, and it stands on its own. We do not go to Lourdes for a new Gospel. We go to hear the old one more deeply.

And what is the message? Prayer. Penance. Conversion for sinners. Come to the water; come together in procession. It is the same as Mary's word at Cana: Do whatever he tells you (John 2:5). At Lourdes the greatest moments are the {Q} and the blessing with the Blessed Sacrament, and many who go home unhealed go home at peace. The water has no power of its own. Bernadette herself said that it would do nothing without faith and prayer.

Today is also the World Day of the Sick. At Lourdes the sick go first, and the healthy push their chairs. Let us ask whether this is so in our parishes and in our homes. Who is sick and alone near us? Who has not been visited? Today let us bring them our prayer, the sacraments and our presence. Our Lady of Lourdes, health of the sick, pray for us. Amen.

cyrilmethodius.t: Monk and bishop, Apostles of the Slavs, co-patrons of Europe
word: And he said to them, “Go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation.”
Mark 16:15
life: Cyril and Methodius were brothers from Thessalonica in Greece, a Byzantine city with many Slav neighbours. Methodius was born about 815 and Constantine, later called Cyril, about 826 or 827. Constantine studied in Constantinople, was admired for his learning and for his gift with languages, and was known as the Philosopher. Methodius served for a time as a civil governor and then became a monk on Mount Olympus in Asia Minor. The two brothers went together around 860 on a mission for the emperor to the Khazars, north of the Black Sea.

About 862, Prince Rastislav of Great Moravia, in what is now Czech and Slovak lands, asked the emperor for teachers who could instruct his people in their own language. The brothers were sent. Before leaving, Constantine devised an alphabet for the Slavonic language, the Glagolitic script, and began translating the Gospels and the liturgy. It was a huge achievement: a people came to have its Scriptures, its prayer and its written language at one stroke.

Frankish clergy working in the region objected, arguing that the liturgy could be celebrated only in Hebrew, Greek or Latin. The brothers went to Rome, bringing with them relics which they believed to be those of St Clement, Pope and martyr, and Pope Hadrian II received them with honour and approved the Slavonic books. Constantine fell ill in Rome and became a monk, taking the name Cyril, and died there on 14 February 869. He is buried in the basilica of San Clemente.

Methodius was consecrated archbishop, with authority over Pannonia and Moravia, and went back. His opponents arrested him and held him in prison for over two years until Pope John VIII obtained his release. He continued the translation of Scripture and died on 6 April 885. After his death his disciples were driven out, but they carried the work to Bulgaria and beyond, and the later Cyrillic alphabet takes its name from Cyril. In 1980 Pope John Paul II named the brothers co-patrons of Europe, and in 1985 he wrote the encyclical Slavorum Apostoli about them.
lessons: God speaks every language
Every people may pray in its own tongue.
Faith that builds culture
An alphabet and a literature were born from the love of souls.
East and West in one Church
Greek missionaries found their support at Rome.
Perseverance in opposition
Methodius kept working through prison and slander.
stories: Do you not all breathe the same air?

His Life says that at Venice Constantine was attacked for using Slavonic in the liturgy. He asked his opponents whether God's rain does not fall on all, and whether the sun does not shine for all, and whether they were not ashamed to allow only three languages.

The accounts of the brothers' visit to Rome say that the Pope received the Slavonic books and had them placed on the altar in the basilica of St Mary Major, and that the liturgy was then celebrated in Slavonic in Roman churches.

The Life of Methodius says that the dying Cyril told his brother that they had been like two oxen ploughing one furrow, that he was falling at the end of the day, and that Methodius must not go back to his beloved mountain, but must complete the work.
quotes: Does not God's rain fall upon all equally? Does not the sun shine on all? Do we not all breathe the air in the same way?
St Cyril, in the Life of Constantine, in substance
p
cyrilmethodius.prayer: O God, you gave the Slav peoples the light of the Gospel through the brothers Sts Cyril and Methodius. Open our hearts to understand your word, and make us a people united in true faith and in right confession. Amen.

points: Good news for the whole creation
No people is outside the Gospel (Mark 16:15).
An alphabet made for love of a people.
They took their work to Rome and found support.
homily: Dear friends, when Prince Rastislav asked for teachers who could speak to his people in their own language, the emperor sent two brothers from Thessalonica. Before they set out, Cyril did something remarkable: he created an alphabet. The Slav peoples could now hear the Gospel and pray the liturgy in their own tongue.

This was not easy. Some argued that God could be worshipped properly only in Hebrew, Greek or Latin. Cyril answered with a simple question: does not the sun shine on everyone? Jesus told the apostles to go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation (Mark 16:15). On the day of Pentecost, people from many nations heard God's deeds in their own languages (Acts 2:6-11). The Gospel is at home in every language.

We should feel this deeply. We pray in Malayalam, in Tamil, in Syriac, in Latin and in English. Scripture in our mother tongue and the {Q} in a language we understand are gifts for which people have worked and suffered. Do we value them? Do we read the Bible in our own language? Do we teach our children to pray in words they understand?

Notice also that these Greek brothers went to Rome. They wanted their work to be in communion with the successor of Peter, and Pope Hadrian approved it. When Methodius was unjustly imprisoned, another Pope obtained his release. Let us thank God for the many ways the one Church prays, and let us ask Sts Cyril and Methodius to help us love both our own heritage and the unity of the whole Church. Amen.

chairpeter.t: Feast of the Apostle's teaching office and of unity with the Successor of Peter
word: And I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.
Matthew 16:18
life: This feast does not celebrate a piece of furniture, and it is not the story of one day in a person's life. In the ancient world a teacher sat in a chair, and a bishop's chair, his cathedra, is the sign of his office of teaching and shepherding his people. To celebrate the Chair of Peter is to give thanks for the ministry that Christ entrusted to Peter for the whole Church. The feast is very old: a Roman calendar of the year 354 already records it on 22 February.

The Gospels show who Peter was. Simon, son of John, was a fisherman of Galilee, a married man (Mark 1:30), whom Jesus named Cephas, or Peter, the rock (John 1:42). When he professed that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of the living God, Jesus said that on this rock he would build his Church, and gave him the keys of the kingdom of heaven and the power to bind and to loose (Matthew 16:16-19). At the Last Supper Jesus told him that he had prayed for him so that his faith would not fail, and that he must strengthen his brothers (Luke 22:32). Peter denied Jesus three times; after the Resurrection, three times he was asked if he loved Jesus and three times he was told to tend his flock (John 21:15-17). In the Acts of the Apostles he leads the first community, preaches at Pentecost and opens the door to the Gentiles.

Christian tradition honours Peter's chair in two cities. At Antioch in Syria, where the disciples were first called Christians (Acts 11:26) and where Paul once opposed Peter to his face (Galatians 2:11), early writers say that Peter was the first to lead the Church. The Syriac tradition honours Antioch as an Apostolic See of Peter and recalls on this date his founding of that see. The Syro-Malankara Catholic Church, which belongs to this Antiochene heritage, therefore has a special reason for joy in this feast. At Rome Peter gave his life by martyrdom under Nero, about the year 64 to 67, and his tomb lies beneath St Peter's Basilica. Before 1960 the Roman calendar kept two feasts, Rome on 18 January and Antioch on 22 February; since then the one feast is kept on this date.

The Catholic Church teaches that the Bishop of Rome, as successor of Peter, is the visible principle of the unity of the bishops and of all the faithful (Lumen Gentium 23; CCC 882). He holds, by Christ's institution, full, supreme and universal power over the whole Church, and all the Churches, East and West, are in communion with him while keeping their own rites and laws. The First Vatican Council in 1870 defined that when the Pope speaks ex cathedra, defining as the supreme teacher a doctrine of faith or morals to be held by the whole Church, he is preserved from error by the Holy Spirit (CCC 891). This does not mean that a Pope cannot sin; Peter himself needed correction and mercy. His office is a service, and St Gregory the Great called himself the servant of the servants of God.
lessons: Christ chose a weak man
The rock was a man who failed and was forgiven.
A ministry for unity
Peter's office exists so that the Church may be one.
Many rites, one faith
Eastern and Western Churches live in one communion with Peter's successor.
Love comes first
Before Jesus entrusted the flock to Peter, he asked: do you love me?
stories: After the Resurrection, by the Sea of Galilee, Jesus asked Peter three times whether he loved him. Peter, who had denied him three times, was hurt and answered that the Lord knew everything. Three times Jesus gave him his flock to care for (John 21:15-17).
When the letter of Pope St Leo the Great was read at the Council of Chalcedon in 451, the bishops, nearly all of them from the East, are recorded to have cried out that Peter had spoken through Leo.

An ancient story says that Peter was fleeing from Rome when he met Jesus on the road. He asked, Lord, where are you going? Jesus replied that he was going to Rome to be crucified again. Peter turned back and went to his martyrdom. Tradition adds that he asked to be crucified head downward.
quotes: With this Church, because of its more powerful origin, every Church must agree.
St Irenaeus of Lyons, Against Heresies III.3.2, on the Church of Rome, in substance
p
The Roman Pontiff, as the successor of Peter, is the perpetual and visible principle and foundation of the unity of both the bishops and the whole company of the faithful.
Second Vatican Council, Lumen Gentium 23, in substance
p
chairpeter.prayer: Almighty God, you have built your Church on the rock of Peter's faith. Grant that no storm may shake us; bless our Holy Father, the Pope, and all our bishops, and keep the whole Church in the unity of faith and love. Amen.

points: We celebrate the office, not the furniture.
Antioch, Rome, and all Churches in one communion.
homily: Dear friends, today we celebrate a chair, and it may seem strange. In the ancient world a teacher taught sitting down, and a bishop's chair came to stand for his ministry. So this is a feast of Peter's ministry: the gift that Christ gave to his Church when he said to a fisherman, You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church (Matthew 16:18).

Think who that fisherman was. He spoke too quickly, he sank in the water, and he denied his Lord three times by a charcoal fire. Jesus knew all this. He told Peter that he had prayed for him, that his faith might not fail, and that once he had turned back he must strengthen his brothers (Luke 22:32). The rock of the Church is not the natural strength of a man. It is the faithfulness of Christ to the man he chose. By the lake he asked only, Do you love me? and then he said, Feed my sheep (John 21:17).

This ministry has continued in the Bishop of Rome. Its purpose is unity. When a Catholic in Kerala, a Catholic in Rome and a Catholic in Syria profess the one faith, it is because of this bond. Our Churches differ in their rites and their history. The Syriac heritage remembers with joy that Peter's chair stood first at Antioch, and the Malankara Catholic Church treasures this link. Rome keeps the memory of his martyrdom and his tomb. These are not rivals. We are one flock, and at every {Q} we pray by name for the Pope.

So let us do three things today. Let us pray for the Pope by name, as for a father carrying a heavy burden. Let us listen to the teaching of the Church with a humble heart, and not only when it pleases us. And let us work for unity in our own parish and family, for those who love Peter's Chair cannot be people who divide. Lord, as you prayed for Peter, keep the faith of your Church from failing. Amen.

polycarp.t: Bishop of Smyrna and martyr, disciple of the apostles
word: Be faithful until death, and I will give you the crown of life.
Revelation 2:10
life: Polycarp was born about the year 69, and he became bishop of Smyrna, the present-day Izmir on the western coast of Turkey. He is a living link with the apostles. St Irenaeus of Lyons, who knew him as a boy, says that Polycarp had been instructed by apostles and had talked with many who had seen the Lord; he remembered Polycarp speaking of his conversations with John. The words of the Book of Revelation to the Church of Smyrna (Revelation 2:8-11), urging it to be faithful until death, came to be fulfilled in him.

St Ignatius of Antioch, on his way to martyrdom in Rome about the year 107, stopped at Smyrna, met Polycarp, and later wrote him a letter full of affection and advice. Polycarp himself wrote to the Church at Philippi, a letter we still have. It is filled with the words of Scripture and with urging to faith, to works of mercy and to perseverance. For the Church of the second century, he was a revered guardian of the apostolic teaching and he stood against those who distorted it.

In his old age, around the year 155, he travelled to Rome to meet Pope Anicetus. They differed over the date of Easter: Polycarp followed the custom of Asia, which he had received from John, and Rome followed its own. Neither persuaded the other, but they stayed in communion, and Anicetus honoured Polycarp by having him preside at the Eucharist in his place. They parted in peace, a lasting model for Churches that differ in custom but share one faith.

Not long afterward, persecution came to Smyrna. The Martyrdom of Polycarp, a letter written by the Church of Smyrna, is the earliest detailed account of a Christian martyr that we have outside the New Testament. Polycarp, then eighty-six or more, was arrested after a servant betrayed his hiding place. He gave food to those who came to arrest him and asked for an hour to pray. Brought to the crowded stadium, he refused to curse Christ, and was condemned to burn. He died about 155 or 156, with a dagger thrust finishing what the fire had not done. The Christians gathered his remains, which they called more precious than jewels, to celebrate the anniversary of his birth into heaven.
lessons: Keeping what was handed on
He passed on faithfully what he had received from the apostles.
Unity in difference
He and Pope Anicetus disagreed and stayed in communion.
Faithful in old age
Holiness does not retire, and his last witness was his greatest.
Kindness to enemies
He fed the men sent to arrest him.
stories: When the proconsul urged Polycarp to curse Christ and go home, the old man answered that he had served Christ for eighty-six years and that Christ had done him no wrong; how could he blaspheme his King who had saved him?

Irenaeus reports that the heretic Marcion once met Polycarp and asked whether he recognised him. Polycarp answered that he recognised him as the first-born of Satan. The story shows how seriously Polycarp took distortions of the faith.

The Martyrdom says that the flames rose around him like the sail of a ship filled with wind, that he stood within them like bread being baked or gold being refined, and that a sweet scent like incense filled the air. When the fire did not consume him, an executioner stabbed him.
quotes: For eighty-six years I have served him, and he has done me no wrong. How can I blaspheme my King who saved me?
St Polycarp, in the Martyrdom of Polycarp 9, in substance
p
Stand fast in these things and follow the example of the Lord, firm and unchangeable in faith, loving the brotherhood and caring for one another.
St Polycarp, Letter to the Philippians 10, in substance
p
polycarp.prayer: God of all creation, you gave St Polycarp a place in the company of the martyrs to share the cup of Christ. Through his prayers, may we hold firmly to the faith handed down from the apostles and stay faithful to you until death. Amen.

points: The word to Smyrna, fulfilled in its bishop (Revelation 2:10).
What Polycarp received, he handed on.
Eighty-six years of service, and no regret.
homily: Dear friends, think of the chain that links us to Jesus. St John knew the Lord. Polycarp knew John. Irenaeus as a boy listened to Polycarp. The faith we profess today has come down through such people, hand to hand. Polycarp is one of the first links in that chain, and we can still read his words.

To the Church of Smyrna the Book of Revelation says: Be faithful until death, and I will give you the crown of life (Revelation 2:10). Polycarp lived that word as an old man. The proconsul offered him an easy way out: curse Christ and go home. He answered that for eighty-six years he had served Christ, who had done him no wrong. How could he blaspheme his King? This is what a long life of faith looks like.

He was also a man of peace. He went to Rome in his old age to discuss the date of Easter with Pope Anicetus. They did not agree, yet they stayed in one communion, and the Pope let him preside at the Eucharist. Our Church knows many customs, calendars and rites. Polycarp reminds us that those can differ as long as we hold firmly to one faith and one communion.

He also fed those who came to arrest him and prayed for them. To our grandparents and elders he says: your last years can be your finest witness. To the young he says: learn the faith from those who have lived it. As we celebrate the {Q} today, let us thank God for those who handed the faith on to us, and let us ask for grace to hand it on, whole and faithful, to those who come after us. Amen.

ranimaria.t: Virgin and martyr, sister of the Franciscan Clarist Congregation
word: No one has greater love than this, to lay down one's life for one's friends.
John 15:13
life: Mariam Vattalil was born on 29 January 1954 at Pulluvazhy, near Perumbavoor in Kerala, into a Syro-Malabar Catholic family of farmers, the second of seven children. Her parents were Paily and Eliswa. She grew up in the ordinary life of a Kerala parish, with family prayer in the evening and a love for the mission of the Church.

In 1972 she joined the Franciscan Clarist Congregation and received the name Rani Maria. She made her first profession in 1974 and her final vows in 1980. Asking to serve in the missions, she was sent to North India, where she worked first at Bijnor in Uttar Pradesh. She also studied social work, so that she could serve the poor with knowledge as well as with love.

From 1992 she worked at Udainagar in the diocese of Indore, in Madhya Pradesh. Many landless tribal families there were trapped in debt to moneylenders and landlords. Sister Rani Maria visited their homes, taught them to read and to save, helped them form groups, showed them the government schemes meant for them, and taught them to know their rights. She did this openly, as a work of faith. Those who profited from the people's poverty began to threaten her.

On 25 February 1995, as she travelled by bus towards Indore, a man hired by her enemies, Samundar Singh, attacked her with a knife on the bus at Nachanbore hill and dragged her out to the roadside, where she died of many wounds, calling on the name of Jesus. She was forty-one. Her killer later repented in prison, and her family forgave him. Pope Francis recognised her martyrdom in March 2017, and on 4 November 2017 she was beatified at Indore, the first woman martyr from India to be declared Blessed. She is buried at Udainagar.
lessons: Faith that serves the poor
She saw no gap between prayer and helping a poor family out of debt.
Courage under threat
She knew the danger and did not leave her people.
Justice as love
Teaching people their rights was part of her love for them.
Forgiveness stronger than death
Her family's mercy to her killer completed her witness.
stories: On the morning of 25 February 1995 she boarded a bus for Indore, at the start of a journey home. Before the other passengers Samundar Singh attacked her, dragged her from the bus and left her dying by the road. Accounts say that she was stabbed more than fifty times and that the name of Jesus was on her lips.

Her younger sister, Sister Selmy, also a Clarist, visited Samundar Singh in prison. On the day of Raksha Bandhan she tied a rakhi on his wrist, the thread a sister gives a brother, and accepted him as her brother. He wept, and he came to repentance.
A son at the family table

After his release Samundar Singh went to Pulluvazhy to ask forgiveness of her family. They received him in their home as a son, and it is reported that her mother kissed the hands that had killed her daughter. He was present at the beatification in Indore.
ranimaria.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you gave Blessed Rani Maria the courage to serve the poor and to lay down her life for them. Through her prayers, make us just to the weak, brave when we are threatened, and ready to forgive those who have wounded us. Amen.

points: An ordinary family and parish gave the Church a martyr.
She laid down her life for her friends, the poor (John 15:13).
Forgiveness made a killer into a brother.
homily: Dear friends, the martyr we honour today is not from a distant century or a faraway land. Blessed Rani Maria was born in 1954 at Pulluvazhy, in a home much like our own homes. Many among us may have known people who knew her. She reminds us that holiness and martyrdom belong to our own time and to our own people.

She went to the poor of Madhya Pradesh and found families trapped in debt. She did not only pity them. She taught them to read and save, to work together and to know their rights. That was what brought her enemies against her. To love the poor sometimes means to stand in the way of those who are growing rich from their poverty, and that has a cost.

Jesus said that no one has greater love than to lay down one's life for one's friends (John 15:13). On a bus on the road to Indore she paid that price, and she died with the name of Jesus on her lips. Yet the story did not end there. Her sister went into the prison and tied a rakhi on the wrist of the killer. Her family received him at their table. Grace won where hatred had seemed to win.

At this {Q} let us remember those we find hard to forgive. Let us ask ourselves who the poor near us are, and whether anyone is cheating them while we stay silent. And let us ask Blessed Rani Maria to give our families her courage and their mercy. Amen.

gregorynarek.t: Abbot and Doctor of the Church, monk and poet of Armenia
word: The sacrifice acceptable to God is a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise.
Psalm 51:17
life: Gregory was born around 950 in the region of Lake Van in historic Armenia, now in eastern Turkey. His mother died when he was small. His father Khosrov, a learned man who wrote a commentary on the Armenian liturgy, became a bishop after her death. Gregory and his brother were entrusted to a relative, Anania, the founder and teacher of the monastery of Narek, on the southern shore of the lake.

He spent almost his whole life at Narek as monk, priest and teacher. It was a time of great flowering for Armenian learning and art under the local princes of Vaspurakan. While still a young man he wrote a commentary on the Song of Songs, and he also composed hymns, odes and a work on the holy cross of Aparank, along with a panegyric on the Blessed Virgin Mary.

His greatest work is the Book of Lamentations, which Armenians often call simply the Narek. It is made up of ninety-five prayers, each described as a speaking with God from the depths of the heart. Gregory stands before God as the worst of sinners, speaks for all humanity, and places his whole hope in the mercy of Christ. Armenian Christians have treasured it for a thousand years, and many have kept a copy in the home and read it beside the sick.

He died around the year 1003 and was buried at Narek. Armenians honour him as a saint and a great poet. St John Paul II praised his writing on Mary in his encyclical of 1987, Redemptoris Mater. On 12 April 2015, at a Mass in St Peter's Basilica marking the hundredth year since the massacres of the Armenian people, Pope Francis proclaimed him a Doctor of the Church. In 2021 his memorial was added to the General Roman Calendar on 27 February.
lessons: Honest prayer
He hid nothing from God, not even the worst of himself.
Hope in mercy
The depth of his sorrow is always met by trust in Christ.
Praying for all
He took the sins of all humanity into his own prayer.
Beauty in the service of faith
His poetry leads the reader to worship.
stories: For centuries Armenian families have kept the Narek in the home. Many have read its prayers over the sick and treated the book itself with great reverence.

A popular Armenian story tells that visitors sent to test him, because he was suspected of error, were served roasted doves on a day of fasting. When they objected, Gregory told the birds to fly, and they rose from the dish alive.

In Armenia in 2016 Pope Francis quoted from the eighty-third prayer of the Narek, where Gregory asks God not to destroy those who persecute him but to change them, a prayer the Pope offered to a people who had suffered so greatly.
quotes: The voice of a wailing heart, its sighs and its cries, I offer up to you, O seer of secrets.
St Gregory of Narek, Book of Lamentations, Prayer 1, in substance
p
Do not destroy those who persecute me, but change them; root out the evil ways of this earth, and plant the good ones in me and in them.
St Gregory of Narek, Book of Lamentations, Prayer 83, in substance
p
gregorynarek.prayer: O God, who gave St Gregory of Narek the gift of speaking with you from the depths of his heart, grant us through his prayers true sorrow for our sins and unshaken hope in your mercy, and teach us to pray for all people, even our enemies. Amen.

points: God does not turn away the heart that is sorry (Psalm 51:17).
Gregory stands before God with all of humanity.
Pray for those who hurt us
Change them, Lord, and change me.
homily: Dear friends, far from Rome, on the shore of a lake in Armenia, a monk wrote prayers that people still read after a thousand years. St Gregory of Narek gave us a book of ninety-five prayers, which he described as speaking with God from the depths of the heart. That is what prayer is, and many of us have rarely dared to pray that way.

Gregory says plainly that he is a sinner. There is no pretending in him. In this season of Lent the psalm says what he says: God does not despise a broken and contrite heart (Psalm 51:17). Sometimes our prayers are polite and careful. We tell God what we think he would like to hear. Gregory teaches us to tell God the truth, and to trust that mercy is greater than any truth we can tell about ourselves.

He goes further still. He does not pray only for himself. He stands before God with the whole human race and takes its sins on his own lips. He even prays for those who persecute him, asking God not to destroy them but to change them, and to plant good things in them and in himself. Those words come from a people who have known terrible suffering.

Today, as we come to this {Q}, let us bring what we have been hiding from God. Let us pray for one person who has hurt us. And let us thank God for the Armenian people, whose faith has been tested by so much suffering, and ask St Gregory to teach us to pray from the heart. Amen.

casimir.t: Prince of Poland and Lithuania, patron of Lithuania
word: For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.
Matthew 6:21
life: Casimir was born on 3 October 1458 in the royal castle at Krakow, the son of Casimir IV, King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania, and of Elizabeth of Austria. With his brothers he was taught by the priest and historian Jan Dlugosz. From youth he was known for his prayer, his simple way of living and his love of the poor.

In 1471, when he was thirteen, his father sent him with an army to Hungary, where a party of nobles had offered him the crown against King Matthias Corvinus. The campaign failed: the soldiers were unpaid and deserted, the promised support did not come, and the Pope favoured Matthias. Casimir returned home. His father, displeased, is said to have confined him for a time in the castle of Dobczyce. He would never again take up that claim.

In the following years he served his father faithfully. Between 1481 and 1483, during the king's long stay in Lithuania, he governed the Polish kingdom from Radom and was remembered for his justice and care for the weak. According to his early biographers, he refused a marriage proposed for him, wishing to remain celibate for the love of God, and he had a deep devotion to the Eucharist and to the Virgin Mary.

Weakened by a disease of the lungs, he died at Grodno on 4 March 1484, aged twenty-five, and was buried in the cathedral of Vilnius, where a splendid chapel was later built over his tomb. He was canonised in the sixteenth century, with the decree confirmed by Pope Clement VIII in 1602. He is the patron of Lithuania and is also honoured in Poland, especially by the young.
lessons: Riches held lightly
A prince's son, he dressed plainly and gave to those in need.
Purity of heart
He kept his heart for God in the midst of a royal court.
Power as service
He used authority for justice and not for his own glory.
Love of Mary
He turned to her every day of his short life.
stories: His early life tells that he would rise at night to go and pray at the door of a church, and that he could be found kneeling there on the ground before it was opened.

A long Latin hymn in praise of Mary, Omni die dic Mariae, is called the Hymn of St Casimir because a copy is said to have been buried with him. He did not write it, but he is remembered as having loved it and prayed it often.

A later legend tells that in 1518, when Lithuanian soldiers came to relieve the besieged city of Polotsk, a young man in white appeared and showed them where to cross the river Dvina. They believed he was St Casimir.
quotes: Every day, every day, sing to Mary, my soul.
Omni die dic Mariae, the hymn associated with St Casimir, in substance
p
casimir.prayer: Lord our God, you gave St Casimir a heart set on the things of heaven in the midst of a royal court. Through his prayers, help our young people to keep pure hearts, and help us all to use what we have in the service of the poor. Amen.

points: The heart goes where the treasure lies (Matthew 6:21).
Rank did not separate him from those in need.
Twenty-five years are enough for a saint.
homily: Dear friends, St Casimir had what many people dream of. He was the son of a king, with wealth, palaces and a future full of power. At thirteen he was already sent with an army to win a crown. Yet he is remembered five hundred years later for something else: for kneeling at the church door before dawn and for his love of the poor.

Jesus tells us that where our treasure is, there our heart will be also (Matthew 6:21). It is a simple test. Where does my mind go when I am not busy? What do I fear to lose? What do I spend my money on? Casimir's treasure was God, and so he could wear plain clothes in a royal court and pass his days without pride.

He also shows us that a holy life does not mean running from duty. When his father gave him the kingdom to look after, he governed with justice and with care for the weak. Those of us with authority at home, at work or in the parish can learn from him. Authority is given so that we may serve.

He died at twenty-five. In this time of fasting, let us pray especially for our young people, who hear on every side that happiness means money, pleasure and success. At this {Q} let us ask St Casimir to help them, and all of us, to put our treasure where it can never be lost. Amen.

word: I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory about to be revealed to us.
Romans 8:18
life: Perpetua and Felicity died for Christ at Carthage in North Africa, in present-day Tunisia, on 7 March 203, under the emperor Septimius Severus, whose decree was directed against new converts. We know their story from one of the most precious documents of the early Church, the Passion of Perpetua and Felicity. It contains Perpetua's own prison diary, the account of a vision by the catechist Saturus, and the words of an editor who wrote down how they died.

Vibia Perpetua was about twenty-two, a well-born and educated young married woman with an infant son at the breast. Felicity was a slave and was expecting a child. They were catechumens, arrested with Revocatus, Saturninus and Secundulus, and they were baptised shortly after their arrest. Saturus, who had instructed them, gave himself up so that he could share their fate.

Perpetua's father, a pagan who loved her dearly, came again and again to beg her to give up her faith, for his sake and for her child's. She suffered deeply for him, but she would not deny Christ. In the prison she had visions: a narrow ladder reaching to heaven with a dragon at its foot, her dead young brother Dinocrates healed through her prayer, and a contest in which she overcame the devil. Felicity feared that she would be held back from dying with her friends, since the law would not allow a pregnant woman to be executed. Two days before the games, after the prayers of the others, she gave birth to a daughter, and a Christian woman took the child as her own.

On the day of the games they went into the amphitheatre with joyful faces. Perpetua and Felicity were thrown down by a wild cow, and Perpetua got up and helped Felicity to her feet. They gave each other the kiss of peace, and then the martyrs were killed by the sword. The names of Felicity and Perpetua are still proclaimed in the Roman Canon of the Mass, and St Augustine preached on their feast at Carthage.
lessons: The first loyalty
Perpetua loved her father and child, and she loved Christ first.
Rich and slave together
In Christ a noblewoman and a slave girl were sisters.
Love in the arena
Even under attack Perpetua stopped to lift up her friend.
The strength of the newly converted
New believers can teach long-time Christians.
stories: When her father begged her to deny her faith, Perpetua pointed to a water jar and asked whether it could be called by any other name than what it was. He said no. Then neither can I, she said, be called anything other than what I am, a Christian.

When Felicity cried out in the pain of childbirth, a jailer mocked her and asked what she would do when she faced the beasts. She replied that now she herself was suffering, but on that day another would be in her, who would suffer for her because she would suffer for him.

The account says that Perpetua, wounded by a trembling young gladiator who struck badly, took his hand and guided the sword to her own throat. The editor says that perhaps so great a woman could not have been killed unless she herself willed it.
quotes: Stand fast in the faith and love one another, and do not let our sufferings be a stumbling block to you.
St Perpetua, to her brother and the catechumens, Passion of Perpetua and Felicity, in substance
p
perpetuafelicity.prayer: O God, for love of whom Sts Perpetua and Felicity defied their persecutors and the torment of death, grant through their prayers that we may hold to you above all things, love one another without distinction, and grow in love for you. Amen.

points: We can be called nothing other than what we are.
Present sufferings are small beside it (Romans 8:18).
homily: Dear friends, we hear the names of Felicity and Perpetua in the Roman Canon, and we may not stop to think who they were. They were two young mothers. One was a lady of good family with a baby at her breast. The other was a slave, who gave birth in prison two days before she died. Perpetua kept a diary, and we can still read it today, in her own words.

Her hardest trial was not the beasts. It was her father, an old man weeping at her feet, begging her to think of him and of her son. Who among us would not have been shaken? She pointed to a jar and said that a thing cannot be called other than what it is: I am a Christian. There are times when we too are asked, gently, by those we love, to be a little less Christian. Perpetua shows us how to love them and remain faithful.

And see them in the arena. The slave and the lady, whom the world had kept far apart, stood together. When Felicity was thrown down, Perpetua lifted her up. Baptism had made them sisters. How do we treat the people in our parish and in our homes who have less than we do? Paul tells us that present sufferings cannot be compared with the glory to come (Romans 8:18). They believed it.

Today, at this {Q}, the same Lord for whom they died is with us. Let us pray for Christians who suffer for their faith today, and for mothers who carry heavy burdens. Let us ask Sts Perpetua and Felicity to help us stand fast in the faith and love one another. Amen.

johnofgod.t: Religious, founder of the Brothers Hospitallers, patron of the sick
word: Truly I tell you, just as you did it to one of the least of these who are members of my family, you did it to me.
Matthew 25:40
life: John Ciudad was born in 1495 at Montemor-o-Novo in Portugal. As a boy of about eight he left home in circumstances that are not clear and ended up at Oropesa in Spain, where he worked as a shepherd. As a young man he served as a soldier for the Count of Oropesa in the wars of the emperor Charles V, and he lived carelessly and lost his faith for a time. He later worked as a shepherd near Seville and as a labourer in North Africa, where he helped a family of Portuguese exiles.

Returning to Spain, he became a seller of religious books and pictures, and around 1538 he opened a small shop in Granada. On 20 January 1539 he heard a sermon by St John of Avila. It pierced him so deeply that he began to cry out in the streets, gave away his books and possessions, and behaved so wildly that people thought him mad. He was taken to the Royal Hospital and treated as the insane were treated then, with chains and whips. There he saw how the sick poor were treated, and he resolved to care for them. John of Avila became his guide.

He rented a house in Granada and began to bring in the sick and homeless, carrying some on his own back and begging for them through the streets at night. He cared for them with his own hands, washed them, fed them and prayed with them. The bishop of Tuy gave him the name John of God and a habit. Friends and followers gathered round him, among them Anton Martin and Pedro Velasco, once bitter enemies.

In 1550, already worn out, he went into a flooded river to rescue a young man from drowning, and he became gravely ill. He died in Granada on 8 March 1550, on his knees, it is said, before a crucifix. His companions became the Brothers Hospitallers of St John of God, approved by Pope St Pius V in 1572, who still serve the sick in many countries, including India. He was canonised in 1690, and he is honoured as a patron of the sick, of hospitals and of nurses.
lessons: God can use a failure
He was past forty, with a wasted life behind him, when he began.
Christ in the sick
Whatever is done for the suffering is done for him.
A guide for the soul
He put his wild zeal under the direction of a wise priest.
Mercy that goes out
He went looking for the poor in the streets at night.
stories: At night John walked through Granada with a basket and pots on his shoulders, calling out: who does good to himself? Do good to yourselves, brothers, for the love of God. He taught that a gift to the poor benefits the giver most of all.

When a great fire broke out in the Royal Hospital of Granada, John ran into the flames again and again, carrying out the sick and throwing bedding from the windows, and came out unharmed. Those who saw it counted it a miracle.
It is told that John was washing the feet of a poor man when he saw in them the wounds of the Lord, and the man told him that all he did for the poor he did for Christ.
quotes: If we look forward to the mercy of God, we shall never fail to do good so long as we have the strength.
St John of God, Letter to the Duchess of Sessa, in substance
p
johnofgod.prayer: O God, who filled St John of God with the spirit of compassion, grant that through his prayers we may serve you in the sick and the poor, and at the last be counted among those you welcome into your kingdom. Amen.

points: A man who failed for forty years became a saint.
The one who gives receives the most.
homily: Dear friends, some saints seem holy from the cradle. St John of God was not one of them. He ran away from home as a boy, worked as a shepherd, went to war, lost his way, and sold books for a living. He was over forty when a sermon broke his heart. If you think your life is already too far gone for God to do anything with it, today's saint has something to say to you.

People thought him mad. He was whipped in a hospital for the insane. But there, among the chained and the beaten, he found his vocation. God often speaks to us from the very place where we have been humiliated. John came out of that hospital resolved that the sick poor should be treated as Christ himself.

Jesus told us this plainly: just as you did it to one of the least of these, you did it to me (Matthew 25:40). John carried the sick on his back, washed them, begged for them at night and called out: do good to yourselves, brothers, for the love of God. It is an astonishing thing to say to a person who is being asked for money. He knew that the giver gains more than the one who receives.

Let us think today of the sick person we have not visited, of the old parent who is a burden, of those who care for the sick in our hospitals and homes. Let us bring them all to this {Q}, and ask St John of God to give us his hands and his heart, while we still have the strength. Amen.

francesrome.t: Wife, mother and widow, religious, founder of the Oblates of Tor de' Specchi
word: She opens her hand to the poor, and reaches out her hands to the needy.
Proverbs 31:20
life: Frances was born in Rome in 1384 into a noble and wealthy family. As a girl she wished to enter a convent, but at about twelve she was married, as her father had arranged, to Lorenzo de' Ponziani, a rich nobleman of Trastevere. On the advice of her confessor she accepted this as God's will. Her marriage lasted some forty years and was a happy one. They had children, and she ran a great household with care.

Together with her sister-in-law Vannozza, who shared her desires, Frances looked for ways to serve God in the midst of family life. They visited the sick in the hospitals of Rome and helped the poor. Her father-in-law at first objected to her giving, but he came to respect her. She kept a simple and penitent life under her fine clothes and treated her servants with kindness.

Her times were hard. The Church was torn by the great schism, and Rome suffered war, plague and famine. When the troops of King Ladislaus of Naples took the city, Lorenzo was badly wounded and later exiled, their property was seized, and their son Battista was taken as a hostage. Plague killed her son Evangelista at the age of nine, and later her daughter Agnes. Frances turned part of her house into a hospital, gave away what she had, and went out with a donkey to gather wood and beg for those in need.

In 1425 she gathered a group of Roman women, still living in the world, as oblates under the rule of St Benedict, attached to the Olivetan monks of Santa Maria Nova. In 1433 they began to live together at Tor de' Specchi, and Pope Eugene IV approved the community. After Lorenzo's death in 1436 Frances joined them as their superior. She died on 9 March 1440 and was buried in Santa Maria Nova, in the Roman Forum, now called Santa Francesca Romana. She was canonised by Pope Paul V in 1608.
lessons: Holiness at home
Family duty came first, and God was found in it.
Suffering turned into mercy
She lost her children and gave her love to the children of others.
Friendship in holiness
Frances and Vannozza encouraged one another for years.
Wealth is for sharing
She kept nothing back when the city was hungry.
stories: It is told that while she was reciting the Office of Our Lady, someone in the household called her away four times on the same verse. Each time she went without complaint. When she returned the fourth time, the verse was written in gold letters on the page.

Her confessor, who wrote down her life and visions, records that for many years she saw beside her an angel, whose light allowed her to read and walk at night. This is why she is named a patron of motorists.
Her early life tells that after she had given away the corn from the family granary to the hungry, her husband and his father found the loft full again, and the empty wine cask full too.
quotes: A married woman must, when called upon, leave her devotions to God at the altar and find him in her household affairs.
Saying attributed to St Frances of Rome, in substance
p
francesrome.prayer: O God, who gave us in St Frances of Rome a model of holiness as wife, mother and widow, grant that through her prayers we may serve you faithfully in every state of life, and find you among the duties of each day. Amen.

points: God is found in household duty.
The strong woman of Proverbs reaches out to the poor (Proverbs 31:20).
Loss can make the heart wider.
homily: Dear friends, many people think that holiness is for priests and sisters. St Frances of Rome wanted to be a nun, and instead she was married at about twelve into a great house. She could have spent her life in regret. Instead she made that house the place where she met God, and she stayed married for forty years.

A saying attributed to her is very simple: a married woman must, when called, leave her devotions at the altar and find God in her household affairs. Mothers and fathers, hear this. Your prayer matters. But the crying baby, the sick parent and the child who needs your time are not interruptions to your life with God. They are part of it.

Frances knew great sorrow. War took her home and her husband's health; plague took two of her children. Sorrow could have closed her heart. It opened her heart instead. She turned her house into a hospital, went out to beg and gathered wood on the road, though she was a noblewoman of Rome. The book of Proverbs says of the worthy wife that she opens her hand to the poor (Proverbs 31:20). There are parents among us who have buried a child. May they know she walks with them.

At this {Q} let us offer our families to God: the good days and the hard days, the meals, the quarrels and the prayers. Let us ask St Frances to teach husbands and wives to love one another faithfully, and to help every Christian home open its hands to those in need. Amen.

word: Go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation.
Mark 16:15
life: Patrick lived in the fifth century; his exact dates are not known. We know his life mainly from two short works he wrote himself, the Confession and the Letter to the soldiers of Coroticus. He was born in Roman Britain, at a place he calls Bannavem Taburniae. His father Calpornius was a deacon and his grandfather Potitus a priest, but Patrick says that as a boy he did not take God seriously.

When he was about sixteen, Irish raiders carried him off with many others and sold him as a slave. For six years he tended animals on the Irish hills, hungry, cold and alone. There, he writes, the Lord opened his mind and he turned with his whole heart to God. He tells us he prayed as many as a hundred times a day, and nearly as many at night. In a dream he was told that a ship was ready. He ran away, walked perhaps two hundred miles to the coast, and at last returned home.

At home he had another dream: a man named Victoricus brought him a letter headed The Voice of the Irish, and he heard them begging him to come and walk among them again. After years of preparation, the details of which are uncertain, he was ordained a bishop and went back to the land of his slavery. He preached, baptised many thousands, ordained clergy and encouraged young men and women to give their lives to God as monks and virgins. He lived in constant danger, and he says he was seized and put in chains more than once.

He was keenly aware of his poor education, and he was hurt when some in Britain criticised him. Yet he defended his people fiercely: when soldiers of the British chief Coroticus killed and enslaved newly baptised Christians, he wrote them a burning letter demanding their release. He died in Ireland, according to tradition on 17 March, and is said to be buried at Downpatrick. Irish missionaries and monks later carried the faith across Europe, and in modern times to Asia and Africa, India among them.
lessons: Slavery became a school
God used his worst years to bring him to prayer.
Forgiving the enemy
He went back to serve those who had enslaved him.
Humble trust
He called himself a sinner and gave God all the credit.
Courage for the weak
He denounced those who enslaved the newly baptised.
stories: In his Confession Patrick tells of a night vision in which he read a letter headed The Voice of the Irish, and heard people near the western sea crying out as with one voice for him to come and walk among them once more.
The fire on the hill of Slane

A life written in the seventh century tells that on Easter night Patrick lit a fire on the hill of Slane, in defiance of a royal command that none should burn before the king's fire at Tara. The king came to confront him, and the Gospel was proclaimed before him.

Popular stories say that Patrick explained the Holy Trinity with a three-leafed shamrock and drove all the snakes out of Ireland. The first appears only many centuries after him, and scholars say the second has no basis, since Ireland had no snakes after the Ice Age. His own writings mention neither.
quotes: I am Patrick, a sinner, most unlearned, the least of all the faithful, and despised by very many.
St Patrick, Confession 1, in substance
p
Christ with me, Christ before me, Christ behind me, Christ in me.
The prayer called St Patrick's Breastplate, traditionally attributed to him, in substance
p
patrick.prayer: O God, who chose St Patrick to bring the Gospel to the people who had once enslaved him, grant through his prayers that we may forgive those who have harmed us, carry the good news with courage, and know that Christ is with us wherever we go. Amen.

points: God met him in his darkest years.
Back to the people who hurt him
All he had he gave to God.
homily: Dear friends, the world remembers St Patrick for parades, green clothes and shamrocks. His own writings tell a far greater story. At sixteen he was seized by raiders and sold into slavery in a foreign land. He had not cared much about God. Now, alone on a cold hillside with the animals, he began to pray, a hundred times in the day and almost as many at night.

Many of us have had a season of pain, of illness, or of a job lost or a family broken, in which all we have is God. We ask why. Patrick discovered that these empty hills can be where we are found. In this time of fasting, when the Church leads us into a kind of desert, we can ask God to meet us as he met that slave boy.

But see what comes next. He escaped, he reached home, he was safe. Then he heard the Voice of the Irish calling him back, the very people who had enslaved him. Who of us would go? Jesus told his disciples to go into all the world and proclaim the good news (Mark 16:15). Patrick went back, in danger, and he gave the rest of his life to them. Forgiveness is not merely a feeling. It may mean walking back to serve those who have hurt us.

He never boasted. He called himself a sinner, the least of the faithful, and he gave all the glory to God. At this {Q}, let us pray for the missionaries who have left home for Christ, many of them from our own Kerala families. Let us ask St Patrick to teach us to pray in hard times and to forgive those who have wronged us. Christ with us, Christ before us, Christ behind us. Amen.

cyriljerusalem.n: St Cyril of Jerusalem (Mar Cyril, Mar Koorilos)
cyriljerusalem.t: Bishop of Jerusalem, Doctor of the Church
word: O taste and see that the LORD is good; happy are those who take refuge in him.
Psalm 34:8
life: Cyril, whom the Syriac tradition calls Mar Cyril or Mar Koorilos, was born around 315, probably in or near Jerusalem. He was steeped in the Scriptures and was ordained a priest. Around 348 he became bishop of the Holy City, at a time when the Church was deeply divided over the teaching of Arius, who denied that the Son is truly God. Because he had been consecrated by Acacius of Caesarea, who leaned towards the Arians, some at first doubted him.
