Before he became bishop, or very early in his time as bishop, he gave the catechetical instructions for which he is best remembered. During the forty-day fast before Easter he taught those preparing for baptism, in the great church that Constantine had built over the place of the Lord's death and burial. He explained the Creed line by line. The lectures to the newly baptised in Easter week, on baptism, the anointing with chrism and the Eucharist, come down to us under his name, though some scholars think that his successor John had a hand in them in their present form. These twenty-four lectures are a priceless window on how the early Church taught and worshipped.

His life as bishop was hard. He quarrelled with Acacius about the rights of his see and was accused, among other things, of selling church goods. Three times he was driven from Jerusalem, and he spent some sixteen years in exile, under emperors who favoured the Arian party. He returned for the last time in 378 to a city torn by faction, heresy and disorder.

In 381 he took part in the First Council of Constantinople, which completed the Creed we profess, and the bishops of the council wrote of him with praise as a true bishop who had fought hard against the Arians. He died in Jerusalem in 386, traditionally on 18 March. In 1883 Pope Leo XIII declared him a Doctor of the Church.
lessons: Know what you believe
He taught people to learn the Creed by heart and to understand it.
Reverence for the Eucharist
He taught that what we receive is truly the Body and Blood of Christ.
Patience in injustice
He bore exile and slander without giving up the faith.
The poor before treasure
He would rather sell church goods than let the hungry starve.
stories: The historians Sozomen and Theodoret record that during a famine in Jerusalem, when the poor had no food, Cyril sold church treasures to feed them. His enemies later used this against him.

In a letter to the emperor Constantius that still survives, Cyril describes a great cross of light that appeared in the sky over Jerusalem on 7 May 351, stretching from Golgotha to the Mount of Olives, and seen by the whole city.

In the lectures to the newly baptised, those coming to communion are told to make the left hand a throne for the right, since it is to receive the King, and to take care not to lose a crumb, as one would never let gold dust fall. Customs of receiving communion differ, but this reverence belongs to all the Churches.
quotes: Do not regard them as mere bread and wine, for by the Lord's own declaration they are the Body and Blood of Christ.
Mystagogical Catechesis 4, attributed to St Cyril of Jerusalem, in substance
p
The Church is called Catholic because it extends over all the world and teaches all the doctrines that people ought to know.
St Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechesis 18, in substance
p
cyriljerusalem.prayer: O God, who through St Cyril of Jerusalem led your Church into a deeper understanding of the mysteries of salvation, grant through his prayers that we may know the faith we profess, hold fast to it in every trial, and receive your holy mysteries with reverence and love. Amen.

points: The Creed is meant to be understood and lived.
The holy mysteries are God's goodness to be tasted (Psalm 34:8).
Truth may cost us our place.
homily: Dear friends, imagine yourself in Jerusalem in the fourth century, in the fast before Easter. You are preparing for baptism, in the great church built where the Lord died and rose again. A bishop stands before you and explains the Creed, line by line. That was St Cyril. Sixteen centuries later we can still read his lessons, because someone wrote them down. How much do we know of the faith that we recite?

He told his hearers that the Creed is to be kept in the heart. Our children learn many things at school. Do they know why we believe that Jesus is truly God? Could we explain it to them? In these last days of the fast, let us take up the Creed at home, go through it slowly, and teach it in our families.

After Easter he spoke of the holy mysteries. He said that what looks like bread and wine are, by the Lord's own word, the Body and Blood of Christ. He taught people to come to communion with reverence, as one receiving a king, and with care not to lose a crumb. And he reminded them of the psalm: taste and see that the Lord is good (Psalm 34:8). Let us look at how we come to {Q}: how we prepare ourselves, how we behave and how we give thanks.

Cyril paid for his faith. He was exiled three times and was slandered, and he was accused even for selling treasures to feed the hungry. He kept going. When we are misjudged for doing right, let us remember him, and ask Mar Cyril to help us know, love and live what we profess, and to feed those who are hungry. Amen.

turibius.t: Bishop, Archbishop of Lima, patron of the bishops of Latin America
word: I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.
John 10:11
life: Turibius was born on 16 November 1538 at Mayorga in Spain, of a noble family. He studied law at Valladolid, Salamanca and Coimbra, and he became a noted teacher of law. King Philip II named him a judge of the court of the Inquisition at Granada, although he was a layman. He was known for his fairness and his upright life.

In 1579, when the great see of Lima in Peru fell vacant, the king chose this layman to be its archbishop, and the Pope confirmed the choice. Turibius protested that he was unworthy and that the canons did not allow it, but he finally accepted. He received the sacred orders one by one, was consecrated bishop in 1580, and landed in Peru the next year, in his early forties. His diocese stretched for thousands of miles along the coast and over the Andes.

He found much disorder: abuse of the native peoples, scandal among some clergy and little instruction in the faith. He travelled his vast diocese three times, on foot and by mule, over mountains and through forests, spending years away from his see. He learned native languages so as to speak with his people, and he defended them against those who oppressed them, which brought him into conflict with officials. In 1582 and 1583 he held the Third Council of Lima, which produced a catechism in Spanish, Quechua and Aymara, the first book printed in South America. In 1591 he founded a seminary at Lima, the first in the Americas under the decrees of Trent.

He is said to have confirmed about half a million people; among them were St Rose of Lima and St Martin de Porres. He fell ill on a visitation and died at Sana on 23 March 1606, which was Holy Thursday, having given away his belongings to the poor. He was canonised by Pope Benedict XIII in 1726. In 1983 St John Paul II named him patron of the bishops of Latin America.
lessons: Called against his will
He obeyed a call he thought himself unfit for.
A shepherd who walks
He went to the sheep, however far they were.
The Gospel in their tongue
He wanted each people to hear Christ in their own language.
Justice for the weak
A bishop has to speak for those who have no voice.
stories: His visitations took him over the high Andes and through regions no bishop had visited. He is recorded as going on foot and by mule, often in danger and sleeping where he could, and spending about seventeen of his years as archbishop away from Lima on these journeys.
When people urged him to rest or questioned why he preached so long and travelled so far, he is said to have answered that time is not our own and that we must give a strict account of it.

He died during his last visitation at Sana, far from his cathedral. It is said that he had himself carried to the church to receive the Viaticum, and that he asked those around him to sing the psalm, I was glad when they said to me.
quotes: Time is not our own, and we must give a strict account of it.
Saying attributed to St Turibius of Mogrovejo, in substance
p
turibius.prayer: O God, who gave your Church increase through the apostolic labours and zeal for truth of St Turibius, grant that those who are consecrated to your service may never tire of seeking the lost, and that your people may grow in faith and holiness. Amen.

points: He lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11).
We shall answer for how we use it.
homily: Dear friends, imagine a lawyer and judge, a layman, being told that he is to be archbishop of a diocese on the other side of the world. St Turibius protested that he was not fit. He obeyed all the same, and he became one of the greatest bishops the Church has ever seen. Many of us know that feeling of being asked for more than we can do. God does not usually call those who feel ready.

Jesus says: I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11). Turibius took this literally. He spent about seventeen of his years on the road, over the Andes, on foot and by mule, to reach people who had never seen a bishop. He learned their languages. He stood up for them against the powerful, and he made sure a catechism was printed that they could read and hear in their own tongues.

He also knew that a Church needs good priests, so he built a seminary, and he called a council to put things in order. Holiness can be very practical. Among those he confirmed were St Rose of Lima and St Martin de Porres. Imagine how much the Church owes to one faithful, overworked man. When we pass on the faith to one child, we do not know what God may do through that child.

He used to say that time is not our own and that we must give a strict account of it. We too shall be asked how we used our time. At this {Q}, let us pray for our bishops and priests, who carry heavy burdens. Let us pray for the people no one visits, and ask St Turibius to help us use the days we have for God and for those who wait for us. Amen.

simeonanna.n: Mar Shem'on and Morth Hanna (Simeon and Anna)
simeonanna.t: The righteous man and the prophetess who met the Lord in the Temple
word: Master, now you are dismissing your servant in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your salvation,
life: On the day after Mayaltho, the Entrance of our Lord into the Temple, the Syro-Malankara Church remembers the two people who were waiting there when Mary and Joseph carried in the child Jesus. All that we know for certain about them comes from a few verses of St Luke (Luke 2:25–38).

Luke writes of Simeon: “this man was righteous and devout, looking forward to the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit rested on him.” The Spirit had revealed to him that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord's Messiah. Guided by the Spirit he came into the Temple, took the child in his arms and blessed God. He called the child a light for the Gentiles and the glory of Israel. Then he told Mary that her son would be a sign opposed by many, and that a sword would pierce her own soul. Luke does not tell us Simeon's age or his work. That he was an old man is the Church's constant understanding, drawn from his words about dying, and that he was a priest is a later tradition.

Anna was a prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. She had lived with her husband for seven years after her marriage and had then remained a widow; Luke gives the figure of eighty-four years. “She never left the temple but worshiped there with fasting and prayer night and day.” She came up at that very moment, praised God, and spoke about the child to all who were looking for the redemption of Jerusalem.

Nothing reliable is known of their lives before or after that hour, and the stories told of them later are tradition or legend. Their place in the Church rests on what they did: they waited, they recognised Him, and they spoke of Him. Simeon's song has been prayed by Christians, East and West, for many centuries, often at the close of the day.
lessons: Faithful waiting
Simeon and Anna kept hope for many years, and God kept His word.
Led by the Spirit
Simeon came to the Temple at the right hour because he listened to the Holy Spirit.
Old age is not useless
God gave two aged people the first sight of the Saviour in His Temple.
Sharing what we have seen
Anna could not keep quiet; she told everyone who was hoping.
stories: When Mary and Joseph brought the offering of the poor to the Temple, an unknown man took the child from them, blessed God and said he was now ready to die. Joseph and Mary, Luke says, were amazed at what was being said about Him (Luke 2:33).

Anna, after long years of fasting and prayer in the Temple, came up at that same moment. She became one of the first to speak about the child to others, to all who were looking for the redemption of Jerusalem (Luke 2:38).

A later Eastern legend says that Simeon was one of the seventy translators of the Hebrew Scriptures into Greek. Coming to the prophecy that a virgin would conceive, he doubted, and he was told he would not die until he had seen it fulfilled. The story has no historical basis, but it shows how the Church loved to think of his long wait.
quotes: The old man carried the child, but the child guided the old man.
An ancient antiphon of the Church for this feast, in substance
p
simeonanna.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, light of the nations and glory of Israel, you came to your Temple and were received by Mar Shem'on and Morth Hanna. Through their prayers teach us to wait for you with patience and to recognise you when you come. Let us receive you with clean hearts, speak of you to all who hope, and at the end depart in peace. Amen.

points: A lifetime of hope is not wasted (Luke 2:25).
The Spirit opens our eyes to a child in His mother's arms.
Anna told all who were waiting (Luke 2:38).
homily: Dear friends, yesterday we kept Mayaltho, when our Lord was brought into the Temple as a child. Today our Church turns to the two people who were waiting for Him there, Mar Shem'on and Morth Hanna. We know them only from a few verses of St Luke, and yet the Church has never forgotten them.

Think how many people passed through the Temple that morning. There were priests, traders and pilgrims, and a poor couple with two birds and a baby. Only two people noticed who that baby was. Simeon saw because the Holy Spirit rested on him. Anna saw because she had spent her life in fasting and prayer. Holiness had trained their eyes.

Simeon took the child in his arms and said: “Master, now you are dismissing your servant in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your salvation.” He was ready to die, because he had seen what he lived for. Do we live in a way that makes us ready to meet the Lord? And Anna went and spoke about the child to all who were looking for redemption. An old widow became a preacher of the Good News.

Let us honour the old people in our families and parishes, whose prayers hold up more of the Church than we know. Let those who are lonely or tired of waiting take courage from these two, because God does not forget a promise. And in the {Q}, when we receive in our hands and on our lips the same Lord whom Simeon held in his arms, let us ask for the same peace and the same joy in telling others about Him. Amen.

ephrem.t: Deacon, Doctor of the Church, the Harp of the Spirit
word: Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly; teach and admonish one another in all wisdom; and with gratitude in your hearts sing psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs to God.
Colossians 3:16
life: Mar Aprem, known in the West as St Ephrem, is the greatest poet and teacher of the Syriac-speaking Church. He was born about 306 at Nisibis, in what is today south-eastern Turkey, probably of Christian parents, though a later Syriac biography says his father was a pagan priest. He grew up under the bishop St Jacob of Nisibis, was ordained a deacon, and taught in the Church of his city. Tradition remembers him as remaining a deacon all his life.

When the Roman Empire handed Nisibis over to Persia in 363, Ephrem left with the Christians of the city and settled at Edessa, today Urfa. There he spent his last ten years teaching. He wrote commentaries on the Scriptures, including Genesis and the Diatessaron, the harmony of the Gospels then read in Syriac churches. Above all he wrote hundreds of teaching hymns, called madrashe, on the Nativity, the Faith, Paradise, the Church, Virginity and the Paschal mystery. Heretics of his day were spreading their errors by songs, and he answered with songs of the true faith.

He teaches not by definitions but through images drawn from Scripture and nature. He loved the Mother of God and praised her purity, and he spoke of the Eucharist as fire and Spirit hidden in bread and wine. According to Palladius, during a famine at Edessa near the end of his life he left his cell and organised relief for the hungry. He died at Edessa in June 373, by tradition on 9 June.

Pope Benedict XV declared him a Doctor of the Church in 1920. The Syro-Malabar calendar keeps his feast on 9 June. The Syro-Malankara Panchangam remembers him in the first week of the Great Fast, on Saturday, together with Mar Theodore the martyr, and in 2027 that falls on 13 February. A short Lenten prayer against sloth, despair, lust of power and idle talk is widely prayed under his name, although scholars doubt that he composed it. Syriac prayer in both our traditions is full of his voice.
lessons: Teaching through beauty
Ephrem shows that a hymn can carry doctrine further than an argument.
Word and worship together
He studied the Scriptures and turned them into prayer for the people.
A refugee who kept serving
Losing his city did not end his work; he began again at Edessa.
Faith that feeds the hungry
The poet left his cell when people were starving.
stories: Jacob of Serugh, writing more than a century later, praises Ephrem for teaching women to sing the faith in church, so that their voices also proclaimed the Gospel. This is one of the earliest accounts of such choirs in the Church.

Palladius, in his Lausiac History, tells that during a famine the wealthy of Edessa would not distribute their grain because they trusted no one. Ephrem offered to do it himself, took charge of the work, cared for the hungry and sick, and died soon after.
The bishop who would not be
A later Syriac life says that when people came to make Ephrem a bishop, he ran through the marketplace behaving like a madman until they went away. The tale reflects the memory of his humility.
quotes: You alone, O Lord, and your Mother are more beautiful than all; for there is no blemish in you, nor any stain in your Mother.
St Ephrem, Carmina Nisibena 27, in substance
p
In your bread is hidden the Spirit who cannot be eaten; in your wine dwells the fire that cannot be drunk.
St Ephrem, Hymns on the Faith 10, in substance
p
O Lord and Master of my life, take from me the spirit of sloth, despair, lust of power and idle talk; give me the spirit of chastity, humility, patience and love.
Lenten prayer attributed to St Ephrem, in substance
p
ephrem.prayer: O God, you made your deacon Mar Aprem a harp of the Holy Spirit to sing the mysteries of your Son. Through his prayers fill our hearts with your word, our mouths with your praise and our hands with mercy for the hungry, so that our lives may be one hymn to you. Amen.

points: What we sing, we come to believe and remember (Colossians 3:16).
The Eucharist is the living God given to us.
True praise goes out to those in need.
homily: Dear friends, today we remember Mar Aprem, a deacon of the fourth century whom the Church calls the Harp of the Spirit. He was never a bishop or a theologian in a great court. He was a teacher in a frontier town, and when that town was lost to Persia he became a refugee. Yet Pope Benedict XV named him a Doctor of the whole Church.

St Paul tells us: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly; teach and admonish one another in all wisdom; and with gratitude in your hearts sing psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs to God” (Colossians 3:16). Ephrem took this seriously. When false teachers spread their ideas through popular songs, he did not only complain. He wrote better songs, taught them to choirs, and the people learned the true faith by singing it.

What do we sing, and what do our children sing? The songs in our homes shape our hearts. Ephrem sang of Mary, of Paradise, of the Birth of the Lord and of the Eucharist. He said that in the bread is hidden the Spirit, and in the cup a fire. When we come to the {Q}, do we come as those who approach fire, with reverence and with love?

And this singer was no dreamer. When famine struck Edessa, he came out and organised help for the hungry, and it seems to have cost him his life. Let us learn from him that praise and mercy belong together. Let us sing the prayers of our Church with attention, read the word of God at home, and share what we have with those who go without. Amen.

addaimari.t: Apostles of Edessa and Mesopotamia, by tradition; fathers of the East Syriac Church
word: After this the Lord appointed seventy others and sent them on ahead of him in pairs to every town and place where he himself intended to go.
Luke 10:1
life: Every Syro-Malabar Catholic knows these two names, because the Holy Qurbana is celebrated for much of the year with the Qudasha of Mar Addai and Mar Mari. Yet very little about the men themselves can be established by history. What we have is the memory of the East Syriac Church, written down long after their time, and it should be read as tradition.

That tradition says Addai was one of the seventy disciples of the Lord, sent after the Ascension by the Apostle Thomas to Edessa, in northern Mesopotamia. Eusebius of Caesarea, writing in the early fourth century, tells the story of this mission, calling the disciple Thaddaeus, and says he drew it from the archives of Edessa. The Syriac Teaching of Addai, from about the year 400, tells it at length with Addai as its hero, including the healing of King Abgar. Historians regard the king's exchange of letters with Jesus as a later composition. What is certain is that Edessa had a Christian community by about the year 200 and became a great centre of Syriac Christianity.

Mari is remembered as the disciple of Addai who carried the Gospel east and south into Mesopotamia and Persia, founding churches around Seleucia-Ctesiphon, where the chief see of the East Syriac Church later stood. The Acts of Mari, the main source, was written centuries afterwards and contains much that is legend. Tradition says he died and was buried at Dorqoni, near Seleucia.

Their greatest monument is the anaphora that bears their names, one of the most ancient Eucharistic prayers still in use. In 2001 the Holy See, with the approval of St John Paul II, recognised its validity even in the old form used by the Assyrian Church of the East, which does not recite the Words of Institution in one continuous narrative; in the Catholic Syro-Malabar and Chaldean use those Words are prayed. Our calendar keeps Mar Addai on the Fifth Sunday of Resurrection and Mar Mari on the second Friday of Kaitha, and the First Qudasha is used from the Monday after Palm Sunday until the end of the season of the Dedication of the Church.
lessons: Sent in pairs
The Gospel travels through people who go together and depend on the Lord.
A debt to unknown missionaries
We have received the faith from those whose lives we hardly know.
A prayer that lasts
What a Church prays shows what it believes, across the centuries.
Honest about history
We may love a tradition and still say plainly what is known and what is not.
stories: The pilgrim Egeria visited Edessa in the 380s. She prayed at the tomb of St Thomas, and the bishop, she writes, gave her copies of the letters said to have passed between Jesus and King Abgar. Whatever the origin of the letters, she shows us how proudly that city then held its apostolic memory.

The story says that Abgar of Edessa, gravely ill, wrote to Jesus asking Him to come. Jesus promised to send a disciple after His Ascension, and Addai came and healed the king, who believed with his people. Eusebius reports the story; historians do not accept the letters as genuine.

The Acts of Mari tell how he went from city to city through Mesopotamia, healing the sick and building churches where shrines had stood. The details are late, but the churches of the East remember him as their founder.
quotes: You put on our humanity to give us life through your divinity; you lifted up our lowliness, raised up our fallen state and gave life to our mortality.
The Qudasha of Mar Addai and Mar Mari, in substance
p
addaimari.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you sent your disciples ahead of you in pairs to every town. We thank you for Mar Addai and Mar Mari and for all who brought the Gospel to the East, and for the prayer that has come down to us with their names. Keep us faithful to the Holy Qurbana and make us bearers of your good news in our time. Amen.

points: Missionaries prepare the way for the Lord (Luke 10:1).
Our Qurbana joins us to the most ancient Churches.
The sending did not end with the seventy.
homily: Dear friends, in this season of the Resurrection our Church remembers Mar Addai, and with him we think of his disciple Mar Mari. We hear their names often, but we know little about them. History tells us that the Gospel reached Edessa and Mesopotamia very early; the stories of how it happened were written down long afterwards. Yet the fruit is plain: a great Church of the East, reaching as far as our own Kerala.

St Luke tells us: “After this the Lord appointed seventy others and sent them on ahead of him in pairs to every town and place where he himself intended to go” (Luke 10:1). Our tradition counts Addai among those sent. Look at the last words of that verse: they go where the Lord Himself intends to go. A missionary does not bring Christ to a place He has forgotten. He prepares for a Lord who is already on the way.

What these men left us is above all a way of praying. The {Q} that we celebrate with their names is one of the oldest Eucharistic prayers in the world. It thanks God that His Son put on our humanity to give us life by His divinity. When we pray it, we stand with Christians who prayed in Syriac under the Persian kings, and with our own forefathers in Kerala.

So let us not treat these prayers as routine. Let us learn what they mean and teach them to our children. And let us remember that the sending has not ended. In our families, at our work, and wherever our people have settled across the world, the risen Lord still sends us ahead of Him, two by two. Amen.

jude.t: One of the Twelve, patron of difficult and desperate causes; feast kept with St Simon the Zealot
word: But you, beloved, build yourselves up on your most holy faith; pray in the Holy Spirit; keep yourselves in the love of God; look forward to the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that leads to eternal life.
Jude 20–21
life: Jude was one of the twelve apostles whom Jesus chose after spending the whole night in prayer on the mountain (Luke 6:12–16). Luke calls him “Judas son of James”; Matthew and Mark name, in the same place in their lists, an apostle called Thaddaeus, and the Church has long understood these to be the same man. That is why he is known as Jude Thaddeus. The Gospels take care to distinguish him from Judas Iscariot, who betrayed the Lord.

John's Gospel keeps one question of his, asked at the Last Supper: “Lord, how is it that you will reveal yourself to us, and not to the world?” (John 14:22). Jesus answered that the Father and the Son will come and make their home with everyone who loves him and keeps his word (John 14:23). After the Ascension, Jude was with Mary and the other apostles in the upper room, devoted to prayer as they waited for the Holy Spirit (Acts 1:13–14).

The short Letter of Jude in the New Testament is written by “Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James” (Jude 1). Tradition has attributed it to the apostle; some scholars think of another Jude, a relative of the Lord. The letter urges Christians to “contend for the faith that was once for all entrusted to the saints” (Jude 3), asks mercy for those who waver, and ends with one of the most beautiful hymns of praise in the Bible (Jude 24–25).

According to ancient tradition, Jude preached the Gospel in Mesopotamia and Persia together with Simon the Zealot, and both died as martyrs there. This is why the Roman calendar keeps their feast together on 28 October. Their relics are venerated in St Peter's Basilica in Rome. In art Jude is usually shown with a club, an axe or a halberd, the instrument of his martyrdom according to tradition, and often with a medallion bearing the face of Christ.

Popular devotion has made him the patron of difficult and desperate causes. A common explanation is that, because his name sounded like the traitor's, Christians for centuries seldom prayed to him, so that he came to be invoked when every other help seemed to have failed. In Kerala, as in many parts of the world, great crowds come to his shrines and to the weekly novena in his honor, bringing their burdens of sickness, debt, unemployment and family trouble.
lessons: An apostle who asked
Jude's one recorded question led Jesus to promise that God makes his home in those who love him (John 14:22–23).
Hidden but faithful
Little is written about him, yet he gave his whole life. Holiness does not need fame.
Guard the faith, show mercy
His letter asks us to contend for the faith and to have mercy on those who waver (Jude 3, 22).
No cause is hopeless with God
True devotion to Jude leads us to Christ, for nothing will be impossible with God (Luke 1:37).
stories: The question at the Last Supper

On the night before he died, Jesus spoke of showing himself to his disciples. Jude asked why only to them and not to the whole world. Jesus answered that the Father and he would come and make their home in everyone who loves him and keeps his word (John 14:22–23).
The face of Christ sent to Edessa

An ancient legend tells that King Abgar of Edessa, who was sick, wrote to Jesus asking him to come and heal him. After the Ascension, a disciple named Thaddaeus was sent to him; the king was healed and many in Edessa believed. Eusebius records an early form of the story in the fourth century; later versions add that Thaddaeus carried a cloth bearing the face of Christ. The story is legendary, but it explains why St Jude is so often shown with the face of Christ on his breast.

Devotion to St Jude spread widely in later centuries. It is often said that St Bridget of Sweden (fourteenth century) was told in prayer to turn to him with great confidence. Ever since, people who had lost hope have prayed to him, and many have given thanks for help received. That is why so many newspapers carry small notes of thanks to St Jude.
quotes: Now to him who is able to keep you from falling, and to make you stand without blemish in the presence of his glory with rejoicing, to the only God our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, power, and authority, before all time and now and forever. Amen.
Jude 24–25
Lord, how is it that you will reveal yourself to us, and not to the world?
St Jude, John 14:22
The Letter of Jude invites us to live our faith with coherence, building ourselves up in it and praying in the Holy Spirit.
Pope Benedict XVI, General Audience on Sts Simon and Jude, 11 October 2006, in substance
p
jude.prayer: Lord God, through the apostles you brought us to the knowledge of your name. By the prayers of St Jude Thaddeus and St Simon, make your Church grow in faith and love; and give to all who are burdened and without hope the help they need, and the grace to trust in you always. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

points: He carried the same name as the traitor, and for centuries few prayed to him. God loves to raise up what others pass by (Psalm 118:22).

Lord, why to us and not to the world? Jesus answers: we will come and make our home with those who love me (John 14:22–23). God does not solve our problems from far away; he comes to live in our house.
Contend for the faith, without giving up
Jude writes to Christians in hard times: build on your faith, pray in the Spirit, keep yourselves in God's love, wait for his mercy (Jude 3, 20–21).
Jude carries the face of Christ on his breast. True devotion includes Confession, the {Q}, perseverance and thanksgiving; it never uses threats or chain prayers.
Become a St Jude for someone
Hope does not disappoint us (Romans 5:5). Visit, help and pray with one person who has lost hope.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, today the Church remembers two apostles, St Simon the Zealot and St Jude Thaddeus. In our land few feasts draw such crowds as this one. People come to St Jude carrying burdens they can no longer carry alone: an illness the doctors cannot cure, a debt that keeps growing, a son who cannot find work, a daughter whose marriage is breaking, a court case that never ends, a child far away who no longer calls. They come because they have heard that St Jude is the saint of hopeless cases. Some of you are here today with such a burden. Let us ask: who is this apostle, and what does he want to teach us?

Jude was chosen by Jesus after a whole night of prayer on the mountain (Luke 6:12–16). His name was Judas, a good and proud name in Israel, the name of the patriarch Judah. But after that terrible night of betrayal, the same name became a shadow. The Gospel writers are careful to say: Judas, not Iscariot (John 14:22). Imagine carrying for your whole life the name of the man who sold the Lord. Perhaps that is why, for many centuries, few Christians prayed to him. The saint who was forgotten became the saint of the forgotten. This is God's way: the stone that the builders rejected has become the chief cornerstone (Psalm 118:22). If you feel forgotten today, by your family, by society, even by God, look at St Jude. God does not forget.

The Gospel keeps only one sentence from Jude's lips. At the Last Supper he asked: Lord, how is it that you will reveal yourself to us, and not to the world? (John 14:22). Perhaps he wanted Jesus to show himself in power, to astonish the crowds, to defeat the enemies. Jesus answered with a quieter and deeper promise: those who love me will keep my word, and my Father will love them, and we will come to them and make our home with them (John 14:23). This is the heart of our faith. Jude does not lead us to a God who solves problems from far away, like an official who signs a file. He leads us to a God who comes to live in our house, in our sickness, in our debt, in our sorrow. Before he changes our situation, he wants to make his home in our heart.

Later Jude wrote a short letter to Christians who were living in hard times, confused by false teachers and tempted to give up. He told them to contend for the faith that was once for all entrusted to the saints (Jude 3). And he gave them four simple instructions: build yourselves up on your most holy faith; pray in the Holy Spirit; keep yourselves in the love of God; look forward to the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ (Jude 20–21). These are not magic formulas. They are the road of a Christian who does not give up: stay rooted in the faith of the Church, keep praying even when the heavens seem silent, remain in God's love, and keep waiting for his mercy. Then he adds: have mercy on some who are wavering (Jude 22). The one who has received hope must pass it on.

So let us honor St Jude in the right way. A novena is not a coin put into a machine to get what we want. It is nine days, or nine weeks, of walking with God in faith. True devotion to St Jude brings us to Confession, to the {Q}, to the Word of God and to works of charity. It perseveres when the answer is slow. It gives thanks when help comes, and it trusts when the answer is different from what we asked. Let us also be clear: chain prayers that threaten misfortune if we do not copy them, or promise success if we publish them a certain number of times, are not Catholic faith; they are superstition. Look at the images of St Jude: on his breast he carries the face of Christ. He never points to himself. He always points to Jesus.

Dear friends, with God no cause is hopeless. Hope does not disappoint us, because God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit (Romans 5:5). And today let each of us become a St Jude for someone else. Somewhere near you is a person who has lost hope: a neighbor in debt, a young person without work, a family in the hospital corridor. Visit them, help them, pray with them. Let us end with the words that close St Jude's letter: to him who is able to keep you from falling, and to make you stand without blemish in the presence of his glory with rejoicing, be glory, majesty, power and authority, now and forever (Jude 24–25). St Jude and St Simon, pray for us. Amen.

jude.a1: Feast sermon: the forgotten saint and the God who comes to live with us

opts.a: In the light of the Word: build yourselves up in faith (Jude 20–25)
points: Build on your most holy faith
Faith is a house built day by day on the rock of Christ (Jude 20; Matthew 7:24).
When we do not know how to pray, the Spirit prays in us (Jude 20; Romans 8:26).
Abide in my love (John 15:9): stay where his love can reach you.
Have mercy on those who doubt; pull them back gently (Jude 22–23).
He is able to keep you from falling
Our strength is not our own; God holds us up (Jude 24).
homily: Dear friends, the Letter of St Jude is one of the shortest books of the Bible, only one chapter. Yet at its end it gives a complete little program for the Christian life: but you, beloved, build yourselves up on your most holy faith; pray in the Holy Spirit; keep yourselves in the love of God; look forward to the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that leads to eternal life (Jude 20–21).

Build yourselves up. Faith is not a feeling that comes and goes; it is a house built day by day. Jesus said that the wise man built his house on rock, and when the rain fell and the floods came, it did not fall (Matthew 7:24–25). We build with prayer, with Scripture, with the Sacraments, with the teaching of the Church. When the storm comes, it is too late to begin the foundation.

Pray in the Holy Spirit. Often we do not know what to ask, or our prayer feels dry. St Paul says that the Spirit helps us in our weakness, for we do not know how to pray as we ought (Romans 8:26). Then keep yourselves in the love of God. Jesus said: abide in my love (John 15:9). We cannot make God love us; he already does. But we can stay where his love reaches us, or we can walk away from it into sin.

Jude also asks us to have mercy on some who are wavering, and to save others by snatching them out of the fire (Jude 22–23). Around us are people whose faith is shaking: a friend who has stopped going to Church, a young person full of doubts. Do not condemn them. Pray for them, listen to them, and gently bring them back.

And finally, the beautiful praise: to him who is able to keep you from falling (Jude 24). Our perseverance does not depend on our strength. God is able to keep us. On this feast let us thank him for the faith that the apostles handed down to us, and at this {Q} let us offer ourselves to him who is able to keep us from falling. Amen.

opts.a: For those who carry heavy burdens: hope when all seems lost
points: Do not worry about anything, but in everything by prayer let your requests be made known to God (Philippians 4:6).
Suffering produces endurance, character and hope, and hope does not disappoint (Romans 5:3–5).
God answers in his own way
My grace is sufficient for you (2 Corinthians 12:9): sometimes he removes the burden, sometimes he gives strength to carry it.
The healed leper returned to give thanks (Luke 17:15–16); our gratitude becomes help for others.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, many of you have come today with a heavy heart. You have prayed, you have tried everything, and still the door has not opened. Some have walked here on foot, some have lit candles, some have made a vow. St Jude understands. That is why he is called the patron of difficult and desperate causes. But what does God want to say to you today?

First: bring everything to God. St Paul writes: do not worry about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God (Philippians 4:6). Nothing is too small or too shameful to bring to him: the debt you hide from your relatives, the addiction in your home, the fear in the night. St Jude prays with you, but it is to God that he leads you.

Second: Christian hope is not wishful thinking. St Paul says that suffering produces endurance, endurance produces character, and character produces hope, and hope does not disappoint us, because God's love has been poured into our hearts (Romans 5:3–5). Hope is not the certainty that everything will go as I want. It is the certainty that God loves me and will not abandon me, whatever happens.

Third: God answers in his own way. Sometimes he removes the burden quickly, and we come back with flowers and thanksgiving. Sometimes, as with St Paul, he says: my grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9). Then he does not take away the cross, but he gives us the strength to carry it, and he carries it with us. Both are answers. Both are love.

Finally: when help comes, do not forget to give thanks. Of the ten lepers healed, only one came back to thank Jesus (Luke 17:15–18). And let your gratitude become help for others. The best thanksgiving to St Jude is not only a notice in the newspaper, but a hand stretched out to someone who is where you were. Go in peace, and know that you are not alone. St Jude, pray for us. Amen.
